name: First Nations of the Subarctic
summary: The Cree, Dene (Athabaskan), Ojibwe, Innu and other nations of the northern forests of Canada and Alaska, who lived by hunting, fishing and trapping for thousands of years and were central to the fur trade.

knownFor.label: Birchbark canoe
knownFor.note: Light canoes that could be carried between lakes and rivers.

knownFor.label: Snowshoes
knownFor.note: Wide frames of wood and hide for walking on deep snow.

knownFor.label: Toboggan
knownFor.note: A flat sled for pulling loads over snow; the word comes from Mi’kmaq.

location.value: A zone of boreal forest of about five million km², running west to east from the Bering Sea to Labrador, south of the Arctic tundra.
location.source: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Subarctic Indigenous Peoples in Canada (checked 13 Nov 2026)

terrain.value: Forests of spruce and pine, many lakes and rivers, the Canadian Shield.

climate.value: Long, very cold winters and short summers.

resources.value: Moose, caribou, beaver, fish, berries, birch bark.

disasters.value: Hard winters and food shortages when animals were scarce.

population.value: Some scholars estimate the whole area may have supported as few as 60,000 people; earlier numbers could have been larger before European diseases arrived.
population.source: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Subarctic Indigenous Peoples in Canada (checked 13 Nov 2026)

urbanisation.value: Seasonal camps; larger summer gatherings at lakes.

disease.value: Smallpox and other epidemics after European contact.

migration.value: Dene peoples moved south (the Navajo and Apache are related Athabaskan peoples).

economicBase.value: People lived by hunting, fishing, trapping and gathering wild plants; some Chipewyan and Dene groups followed the caribou herds, and fish were caught with nets, traps, spears and hook and line.
economicBase.source: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Subarctic Indigenous Peoples in Canada (checked 13 Nov 2026)

tradeRoutes.value: Exchange networks; from 1670 trade with the Hudson’s Bay Company.

wealth.value: Wealth meant skill, sharing and kinship ties.

moneyAndTax.value: None; later furs were traded for goods.

governmentType.value: No state; family bands led by respected hunters and elders.

keyRulers.value: No rulers were recorded in early times.

succession.value: Leadership came from ability and respect.

stability.value: Bands moved with the seasons and animal herds.

eliteConflict.value: Disputes were settled within kin groups.

majorWars.value: Conflicts between nations; later the North-West Rebellion (1885) involved some Cree.

territoryChange.value: Signed the Numbered Treaties with Canada (1871–1921).

alliancesRivals.value: Allied as trade partners with the Hudson’s Bay Company.

scienceEducation.value: Knowledge of land and animals passed on orally; Cree syllabics invented in the 1840s.

openness.value: Adopted guns, metal tools and trade goods.

communicationTransport.value: Canoes in summer, snowshoes and toboggans in winter.

religion.value: Spiritual beliefs about animal spirits; later Christianity.

languageWriting.value: Western Subarctic peoples are generally Athapaskan (Dene) speakers; most Indigenous peoples of the Eastern Subarctic speak Algonquian languages.
languageWriting.source: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Subarctic Indigenous Peoples in Canada (checked 13 Nov 2026)

sharedIdentity.value: Separate nations with their own identities.

dailyLife.value: Cone-shaped lodges of poles covered with birch bark or hides; moose meat, fish and pemmican.

neighbours.value: Inuit to the north, Plains peoples to the south, later fur traders.

ideasReligions.value: Traditional beliefs, then Christian missions in the 19th century.

colonisation.value: Lands came under Canada; residential schools caused lasting harm.

riseSignals.value: Skilled adaptation to the northern forest.

declineSignals.value: Epidemics and loss of land after contact with Europeans.

outcome.value: Early contact in the 17th century caused migration, especially among the Cree; fur traders were active after Alexander Mackenzie’s voyages from 1789, and the Hudson’s Bay Company took over North West Company posts in 1821. The article does not give the earliest date of human presence.
outcome.source: The Canadian Encyclopedia: Subarctic Indigenous Peoples in Canada (checked 13 Nov 2026)

overallCertainty.value: Known from archaeology, oral history and fur-trade records.
